metadata.title: Ted Cruz Calls JD Vance ‘Insecure’ as GOP Presidential Race Heats Up

sources.news_title: Ted Cruz vs JD Vance: 2028 Presidential Race Heats Up
sources.text:
Sen. Ted Cruz told Politico that JD Vance is "feeling insecure" after the vice president claimed the Texas senator is already running for 2028.
The public clash between two possible Republican contenders spilled into the open after Vice President JD Vance told NBC News on Thursday that Cruz is plainly already in the next presidential race, while Cruz answered two days later that political bomb-throwing usually comes from insecurity.
Fox News reported the exchange as both men keep a heavy midterm travel schedule and leave the door cracked on 2028. Cruz insists his focus is winning in November. Vance says the same about electing Republicans right now.
The dispute is simple on its face. Vance cast Cruz as a candidate already. Cruz cast Vance’s charge as a sign of nerves. Neither man used the moment to declare a presidential bid of his own.
In the Thursday NBC News interview, Vance did not hedge.
Vance told NBC News:
"It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president."
He drew a hard line on his own plans in the same breath.
Vance also said:
"At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans. That’s what I’m going to keep on doing."
That framing puts the vice president in the role of party workhorse while tagging the Texas senator as the one already looking past the midterms. It also lands in a climate where Usha Vance has discussed a possible 2028 bid and polling talk around Vance keeps rising.
Cruz took the call from Politico on Saturday and did not let the shot pass.
Cruz told Politico:
"In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure."
He added that Vance can say what he wants, then steered straight back to the calendar.
Cruz said:
"So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes."
And:
"I’m going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days."
Cruz has left the 2028 door open before. In August he told MS NOW he would “certainly be part of the discussion.” He ran for the GOP nomination in 2016. He has not announced a new presidential campaign now, and he is using the Vance exchange to argue that House and Senate control come first.
Cruz’s defense rests on volume of help for other Republicans. He told Politico no Republican has campaigned for more Senate, House, and gubernatorial candidates over the last 10 years, and he said this year will match that record.
"Over the last 10 years, there’s no Republican in the country who has campaigned for more Senate candidates, more House candidates, more gubernatorial candidates than I have, and this year will be no exception."
He pointed to recent and planned stops in Georgia, Iowa, Nebraska, South Carolina, and Ohio, with more travel this month to Alaska, Florida, North Carolina, and South Carolina. On Sept. 10, 2026, he spoke on the second day of the Republican Midterm Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas.
Vance has been on the road too. He campaigned in Texas and Florida last week and was set for a Monday rally in Alaska. On Sept. 30, 2026, he spoke at the Harlingen Convention Center in Harlingen, Texas, at a rally meant to boost local Republican candidates, including Eric Flores in Texas’ 34th Congressional District. That kind of surrogate work sits alongside wider speculation about who might join a Vance ticket in 2028.
Cruz also reached for shared history. He noted that he spent a full day campaigning with Vance during the Ohio Senate race Vance won in 2022.
"Indeed, ironically, I spent a full day on the road with JD Vance, campaigning with him when he was running for Senate in Ohio."
He followed with a plain endorsement of that outcome.
"I was very glad he won that race. I was very glad to help him."
The line serves a political purpose. It paints Cruz as a team player who invested in Vance’s rise, and it makes the vice president’s “already running” claim look ungrateful in Cruz’s telling. Vance, for his part, has kept pressing core conservative issues on the trail, from Big Tech’s use of H-1B visas to border failures he has tied to family breakdown back home in Ohio.
None of that resolves the 2028 question. Cruz has not said he is in. Vance has said he is not in “at this moment.” Both keep showing up for Republican candidates anyway. Cruz’s June 10, 2026, turn at a Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee roundtable on college sports in the Russell Building showed the same dual track, governing work by day, political positioning never far from the surface.
Party activists watching the exchange see two ambitious conservatives who may one day face each other, even while they still need each other for November. Vance has also had to swat away personal shots on the trail, including when he rebuked personal comments about his wife at a Michigan event, another reminder that the modern campaign lane stays rough whether the race is a midterm or a presidential trial heat.
Cruz’s message is that insecure politicians throw bombs and secure ones grind out wins for the conference. Vance’s message is that Cruz’s presidential machinery is already visible and that his own job is electing Republicans in the cycle still in front of them. Voters get to test both claims against the travel logs and the November results.
Midterms punish parties that get lost in the next race before they finish the current one, and Republicans who want the House and Senate should measure every speech by that standard.

sources.news_title: Cruz-Vance Feud Ramps Up After Cruz Says VP Is 'Feeling Insecure'
sources.text:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) accused Vice President JD Vance of being “insecure” after Vance said it was “really obvious” Cruz is planning a 2028 presidential run.
“In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure,” Cruz said of Vance during a phone interview with Politico on Saturday. “So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes.”
Cruz rejected the claim that he is actively campaigning for the White House at this moment, adding, “I’m going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days.”
Vance, also a Republican, initially made the remark about Cruz to NBC News last week.
“It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance told the outlet on Oct. 1. “At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans. That’s what I’m going to keep on doing.”
Weeks before, Cruz, who ran for president in 2016 and has publicly mused over running again in 2028, told MS NOW in August that the Republican Party hasn’t automatically united around Vance as President Donald Trump’s successor. Vance and Cruz have widely been considered as anticipated rivals for the 2028 Republican presidential primary.
Cruz, who isn’t up for reelection this year, made the assessment after MS NOW’s Ali Vitali asked if the party had settled on Vance, to which Cruz replied, “Oh, no. There’s going to be a full discussion about who we are and what we believe.”
“I’ll certainly be part of the discussion,” he added. “Economically, I think we should be a conservative party, and on foreign policy, we’ve got a debate: Are we an isolationist party that withdraws from the world, or do we believe in American leadership? And I care deeply about both of those issues and who the party is.”
As for Vance’s remark about Cruz, a spokesperson for the Texas senator stressed that Cruz’s current focus is securing votes for Republicans for the November midterms.
“Senator Cruz has been focused on electing Republicans up and down the ballot this November, and he will continue campaigning vigorously over the next several weeks to help make that happen.” the spokesperson said in a statement to NBC News.
Although neither politician has formally announced a campaign, Vance leads early 2028 Republican primary polls and prediction markets against other potential Republican contenders, including Cruz.
According to Kalshi’s 2028 Republican nominee prediction market, Vance has a 45% implied chance of securing the GOP nomination, while Cruz sits at a just above 2% chance.

sources.text:
Ted Cruz Calls Out JD Vance as 'Insecure' After VP Says It's 'Really Obvious' the Texas Republican Is Running for President
Oct. 4 2026, Updated 2:40 p.m. ET
Sen. Ted Cruz fired back at J.D. Vance after the Vice President suggested the Texas Republican is already positioning himself for a 2028 presidential campaign, RadarOnline.com can reveal.
Cruz accused Vance of being "insecure" while maintaining that his attention is currently on helping Republicans in the midterm elections.
JD Vance Calls Out Ted Cruz
On October 1, Vance addressed Cruz's political ambitions during an NBC News interview.
"It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president," Vance said. "At this moment, I'm not. I'm trying to help elect Republicans. That's what I'm going to keep on doing."
In response, a spokesperson told the outlet, "Senator Cruz has been focused on electing Republicans up and down the ballot this November, and he will continue campaigning vigorously over the next several weeks to help make that happen."
Ted Cruz Fires Back
Two days after Vance's remarks, Cruz responded during a phone interview with Politico.
"In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they're feeling insecure," Cruz said.
"So he's welcome to make whatever comments he likes. I'm going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days," he added.
Ted Cruz Left Door Open to 2028 Run
Cruz has previously made it clear that he is not ruling out a White House bid.
During an August interview with MS NOW, the senator rejected the suggestion that the GOP had already chosen Vance.
Cruz said his party will "have to decide who we are, what we do believe."
He added, "There will be time to figure that out. I'll certainly be part of the discussion."
Ted Cruz's 'Endorsement Philosphy'
During his MS NOW interview, the Texas republican also shed light on how he chooses a candidate to stand behind.
"My philosophy on endorsements is I support the most conservative candidate who can win," Cruz shared. "I look at, No. 1, what's their record? Have they been a conservative? Have they been principled?"
Cruz also praised Donald Trump, calling him "an extraordinary president."
"Trump doesn't hide in the corner. He is ferocious. I like that," Cruz explained. "I wish sometimes there was more message discipline and focus. And so, for 10 years, I mean, I talk to him every week, sometimes every day, and I try to urge him to do good things and urge him not to do bad things. And he doesn't always listen to me, but he frequently listens to me."

sources.news_title: What Did Ted Cruz Say About JD Vance's Claim?
sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance and Sen. Ted Cruz are now trading public remarks about who is, and who is not, already running for president in 2028. Vance said Thursday that Cruz’s current posture makes a White House bid plain to see. Cruz answered Saturday by tying those remarks to insecurity and to what he called political bomb-throwing.
The back-and-forth surfaced in two separate interviews. Vance spoke with NBC News, and Cruz later spoke by phone with POLITICO. Both men are treated as possible contenders for the next Republican presidential nomination, and both said their immediate priority is electing other Republicans.
Cruz did not deny interest in a future race, but he said the next 30 days belong to the midterms. “In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure,” he told POLITICO. “So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes. I’m going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days.”
Vance’s NBC remarks and Cruz’s record of campaign stops
Vance’s comment came during the Thursday NBC News interview. He drew a line between Cruz’s activity and his own. “It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance said.
“At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans. That’s what I’m going to keep on doing. It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance said.
Vance is widely viewed as the frontrunner for the Republican nomination. Cruz has pushed back on the idea that the nomination is already settled. He has also left the door open to his own bid. “I’ll certainly be part of the discussion,” he told MS NOW in August.
In the Saturday interview, Cruz framed his schedule as proof that the midterms come first. He said he has already campaigned with Republican candidates in Georgia, Iowa, Nebraska, South Carolina, and Texas. He added that more trips are set this month in Alaska, Florida, North Carolina, and South Carolina.
He also cast this year’s travel as a continuation of earlier cycles, not a new turn toward 2028. “Over the last 10 years, there’s no Republican in the country who has campaigned for more Senate candidates, more House candidates, more gubernatorial candidates than I have, and this year will be no exception,” he said. He said the goal is helping Republicans hold both chambers of Congress.
Cruz then named people he said he has boosted in past races, including former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and U.S. House candidate Karoline Leavitt. He put Vance on that same list. Cruz’s history of backing Vance now sits against a 2028 backdrop in which Trump has publicly kept the race open but reportedly told donors privately to back Vance.
“Indeed, ironically, I spent a full day on the road with JD Vance, campaigning with him when he was running for Senate in Ohio [in 2022],” Cruz said. “I was very glad he won that race. I was very glad to help him,” he also said.

sources.news_title: Republican 2028 presidential frontrunners as Cruz slams 'insecure' Vance
sources.text:
Sen. Ted Cruz has accused Vice President JD Vance of being "insecure" during a phone interview with Politico, after the two prominent Republicans traded barbs over speculation about the 2028 presidential race, highlighting growing attention on a contest that remains more than two years away.
The exchange comes as prediction markets place Vance firmly ahead of the rest of the potential Republican field, illustrating his status as the early favorite to succeed President Donald Trump should he seek the GOP nomination in 2028.
What Happened?
The disagreement began after Vance told NBC News that it was "really obvious" Cruz was already running for president, while adding that his own focus remained on helping to elect Republicans.
"I'm trying to help elect Republicans. That's what I'm going to keep on doing," Vance said.
Cruz responded sharply during an interview with Politico, which was published on Saturday.
"In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they're feeling insecure," Cruz said. "So he's welcome to make whatever comments he likes. I'm going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days."
The Texas senator also pushed back on suggestions that he’s prioritizing a White House bid, pointing instead to the traveling he’s doing on behalf of Republican candidates around the country.
Cruz told Politico he’s campaigned for GOP candidates in states including Georgia, Iowa, Nebraska and South Carolina, with additional events planned in Alaska, Florida and North Carolina.
Vance Leads 2028 Republican Field
While neither man has formally announced a presidential campaign, prediction markets currently show that Vance has a rather significant advantage over other potential Republican contenders, including Cruz.
On Polymarket's Republican nominee market, Vance was trading at roughly 50 percent, far ahead of Secretary of State Marco Rubio at about 15 percent, and Cruz at 3 percent.
A similar picture emerges on Kalshi.
The exchange's 2028 Republican nominee market showed Vance with about a 44 percent implied chance of securing the GOP nomination, compared with roughly 20 percent for Rubio, with Cruz coming in at just above 2 percent.
Why It Matters
This recent public clash is one of the clearest signs that there’s increasing tension among Republicans, all fighting to emerge as leading contenders in a post-Trump presidential race.
Vance is widely regarded as Trump's political heir and has benefited from the visibility that comes with serving as vice president. Meanwhile, Cruz remains one of the best-known conservatives in the Senate and has maintained a national political profile since his own 2016 presidential campaign.
Cruz has previously indicated that he doesn’t view Vance as an inevitable nominee, telling MS NOW earlier this year that he would "certainly be part of the discussion" over the Republican Party's future leadership.
The senator also noted that he had campaigned heavily for Vance during his successful 2022 Senate run in Ohio, telling Politico that, "ironically, I spent a full day on the road with JD Vance, campaigning with him when he was running for Senate in Ohio," adding that he was "very glad he won that race. I was very glad to help him."
What Happens Next
Although most Republicans will undoubtedly remain focused on the 2026 midterm elections, this latest heated exchange shows that, for some, the attention is already shifting toward the next presidential cycle.
For now, betting markets suggest Vance is the clear frontrunner for the 2028 Republican nomination, with Rubio a distant second and a large field of other prospective candidates—Cruz being one of them—trailing behind.
Whether that advantage holds as the party moves beyond the midterms and closer to the next presidential campaign remains to be seen.
Newsweek has reached out to both Vance and Cruz for comment and is awaiting a response.

sources.text:
Ted Cruz fires back at ‘insecure’ JD Vance as the two trade barbs over 2028
WASHINGTON — Texas Sen. Ted Cruz fired back at Vice President JD Vance for suggesting he is already gearing up for a 2028 bid — blasting the veep as “insecure.”
Vance, widely seen as the 2028 frontrunner, threw shade at Cruz (R-Texas) last week when he implied that the Lone Star State lawmaker was more focused on 2028 than the upcoming midterms.
“In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure,” Cruz snapped back in an interview with Politico on Saturday.
“So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes,” Cruz, 55, continued.
“I’m going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days.”
Cruz had been the second-place finisher in 2016 against President Trump, following a bitter and bruising fight.
Back in August, Cruz told MS NOW that he would “certainly be part of the discussion” in 2028 and suggested that Vance doesn’t have a lock on the 2028 GOP nod.
“It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance responded to the jab in an interview with NBC News.
“At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans. That’s what I’m going to keep on doing.”
Many Republicans see the 2028 presidential election cycle as an opportunity to dramatically recalibrate the GOP after Trump. Traditionalists like Cruz want the GOP to return to its roots of free markets and fiscal restraint.
Meanwhile, MAGA Republicans want the party to remain in a populist direction and recommit to staying out of foreign entanglements.
Cruz, who has previously reminisced about his prior presidential run, has already engaged in some of those battles over the future of the GOP, sitting down with nicotine-pouch salesman and podcast giant Tucker Carlson for a fiery clash in June of last year.
Carlson and Vance have long been chummy, despite the veep acknowledging some recent political differences with the pundit, who has turned on Trump.
The Texas Republican crowed about his efforts to boost Republican candidates heading into the Nov. 3 midterm elections, where his home state is in play for a tough Senate race.
“Over the last 10 years, there’s no Republican in the country who has campaigned for more Senate candidates, more House candidates, more gubernatorial candidates than I have, and this year will be no exception,” Cruz vowed to Politico.
“Indeed, ironically, I spent a full day on the road with JD Vance, campaigning with him when he was running for Senate in Ohio [in 2022],” the senator added. “I was very glad he won that race. I was very glad to help him.”
The Post contacted Vance’s team for comment.

“He’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes. I’m going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days.”

Cruz also argued that Vance was the one allowing himself to become distracted, pointing out that no Republican had campaigned for more candidates than he had over the past decade. He added that this year would be no different.
The Texas senator cited more than a dozen candidates he successfully supported during his time in the Senate, including Vance.
“Indeed, ironically, I spent a full day on the road with JD Vance, campaigning with him when he was running for Senate in Ohio [in 2022],” Cruz said.
Ted Cruz labeled JD Vance “insecure” after the vice president said it was “really obvious” the Texas senator was running for president, escalating the public clash between the two Republican figures
Vance was responding to Cruz’s August claim that Republicans had not yet united behind the vice president as their 2028 presidential nominee
“I was very glad he won that race. I was very glad to help him,” Cruz said.
Our News Outlet has contacted Vice President Vance for comment.
The latest dispute between Cruz and Vance resurfaced when reporters asked the vice president Thursday about the upcoming midterms and whether the GOP’s election result would influence his decision to seek the presidency.
“Regardless of what happens over the next 35 days, there will be new information, new things you have to make a decision over,” Vance replied.
Vance has not declared a presidential candidacy and has remained guarded about his plans. Asked about the possibility, he brushed it aside by saying, “The American people make that decision.”

The vice president then turned his attention to Cruz, a former Senate colleague.
“It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance told NBC News.
“At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans. That’s what I’m going to keep on doing.”
Cruz pointed to his record of campaigning for dozens of Republican candidates, including Vance during his 2022 Senate campaign in Ohio
Cruz said in August that neither he nor the Republican Party had united behind Vance as the GOP’s 2028 candidate, insisting that the nomination discussion remains open.
‘Oh, no. There’s going to be a full discussion about who we are and what we believe,’ Cruz said. ‘I’ll certainly be part of the discussion.’
The Texan accused Vance of being an acolyte of Tucker Carlson, the podcaster and former Fox News host, according to Axios.
Cruz and Carlson have clashed and traded insults, particularly over the Texan’s strong support of Israel.
Vance and Cruz were Senate colleagues long before Vance’s nomination to become Trump’s running mate.
Cruz was Trump’s most formidable GOP challenger in the 2016 campaign, and he was the last to drop out after Trump received 45 percent of the Republican backing while the Texan received just 25 percent.
While Cruz is not on the ballot this year – his term runs through 2030 – he has been campaigning in swing states, including Iowa and South Carolina, both early presidential primary states, to fundraise for the GOP ahead of this year’s elections.
The Texas senator’s presidential ambitions are seen as a long shot.
Vance currently has a 45 percent chance of becoming the GOP’s 2028 presidential nominee, according to the prediction market Kalshi.
Cruz, meanwhile, has just a two percent chance.

sources.news_title: ‘Insecure’ JD Vance targeted by MAGA senator as 2028 contenders trade blows: report
sources.text:
A simmering rivalry between two Republican heavyweights eyeing the White House spilled into public view this week, with one making it personal.
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) called Vice President JD Vance "insecure" in a phone interview with Politico on Saturday, responding to Vance's claim days earlier that the Texas senator was already running for president.
"In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they're feeling insecure," Cruz said. "So he's welcome to make whatever comments he likes. I'm going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days."
The jab followed an NBC News interview Thursday in which Vance accused Cruz of jumping the gun on a 2028 bid while the party fights to hold Congress.
"It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president," Vance said. "At this moment, I'm not. I'm trying to help elect Republicans. That's what I'm going to keep on doing."
Vance is widely seen as the early favorite for the GOP nomination, but Cruz has openly questioned whether the vice president has it locked up and has floated a run of his own. "I'll certainly be part of the discussion," Cruz told MS NOW in August.
Cruz insisted to Politico that his attention is on keeping Republican majorities in the House and Senate, pointing to campaign stops this cycle in Georgia, Iowa, Nebraska, South Carolina and Texas. He said he plans to stump for candidates in Alaska, Florida, North Carolina and South Carolina later this month.
"Over the last 10 years, there's no Republican in the country who has campaigned for more Senate candidates, more House candidates, more gubernatorial candidates than I have," he said. "And this year will be no exception."
A spokesperson for Vance did not immediately respond to Cruz's remarks, per Politico. Vance campaigned in Texas and Florida this week and is set to hold a rally in Alaska on Monday.
